slides.title: AI Prompting for Scholarship Review
slides.lead: Everyday language, clear examples, and practice in ChatGPT
items: Miguel Guhlin
NSPA 2026 · October 21
slides.notes: I will begin with the everyday meaning of AI and prompting. You do not need to know technical terms or write code to take part. I will show a short request first, then add only the information that helps us get a useful answer. After that, we will use three made-up applications to practice office tasks. You can copy the prompts from the practice page, and you can compare the answer with the original files. I will keep responsibility clear: AI prepares a draft or checklist, and a person checks it and makes the decision.

slides.title: My starting point
slides.lead: Eight short situations, a score, and a graph
items: What would I do in each situation?
Which idea would I like to practice?
slides.notes: I invite you to take the awareness self-check before we begin. It uses eight everyday situations, including checking an AI answer and deciding what information we may upload. The result shows a score out of eight, a graph of your answers by topic, and short suggestions for improvement. The guided ChatGPT activities are separate. This is a workshop activity, not a test of your qualifications. Your answers stay on the page and are not sent to anyone. The score is easy to note for later reference. You can return after the demonstrations and see which choices make more sense.

panels: Eight everyday situations about using AI carefully.
Find out which topics need more attention.
Get clear ways to improve based on your answers.
infographic.alt: A three-stop learning path: a hand chooses one of three large unlettered answer circles beside a question sheet; a person studies a sheet and magnifying glass; a person tries one small task with a laptop. Clear connecting arrows. No score, no expertise badge.

slides.title: What generative AI does
slides.lead: It creates a draft from your request and the information available to it.
items: It can help write, summarize, and organize.
It can also leave things out or add incorrect details.
slides.notes: Generative AI is software that creates something, such as text or an image, from a request. In this workshop, I will use ChatGPT to work with text and files. Think of the answer as a draft that needs your attention. A useful draft may save us time, but fluent writing does not tell us whether every detail is correct. We need to look at the information we supplied and compare it with the answer. I am going to keep our first example small enough that everyone can do that comparison without opening a complicated packet.
slides.alt: A person sends a request and receives an AI draft.

panels: Say what you want AI to help you do.
Add the facts or files the task needs.
Compare the answer with the original.
infographic.alt: A speech bubble containing a pencil request at left, an open source notebook and table sheet in the middle, a computer showing a draft page at right with a human hand and magnifying glass checking it. Arrows connect the request and source information to the draft. Not a robot. Do not imply every request requires files.

slides.title: Words for our first chat
slides.lead: A prompt is simply your request.
table: The app you talk with, such as ChatGPT
The AI system the app uses to create an answer
Your request and the information you give it
The answer or draft you receive
slides.notes: These words describe things you will see as we work. A chatbot is the app where the conversation happens. A model is the AI system the app uses to create an answer. A prompt is your request. Input includes that request and any information you provide, such as a note or an attached file. Output is what comes back. I will usually say request and answer because those words are enough for our exercises. You do not need a special formula. Clear everyday language is a good place to start, and you can follow up when an answer needs changing.

slides.title: A first request
slides.lead: One small job using a made-up note
items: No real applicant information is needed.
I can check the date and length myself.
slides.quote: Using this note only, write a friendly one-sentence reminder: “Applications close October 1.”
slides.notes: I will open a fresh ChatGPT chat and type this request. The note is made up for practice. We want a friendly reminder, one sentence long, and we want the deadline to stay October 1. I will pause before sending so you can see the whole request. After the answer appears, I will read it with you. Did it keep the date? Did it stay within one sentence? Did it add any new rule or promise? If the live tool is unavailable, the practice page has a clearly labeled prepared example we can inspect together.

panels: Keep October 1. Add no new rules or promises.
infographic.alt: At left a large paper note and calendar showing a blank deadline square, center a writing hand drafts a single-line reminder on a sheet beside a friendly person, right a magnifying glass checks the calendar and a short one-line reminder. Connected arrows. No real applicant data, dates, letters or numbers.

slides.title: Useful background information
slides.lead: Context means the information that helps AI do the job.
table: No invented dates, links, or promises
slides.notes: Context means useful background information. For this reminder, the audience is the students who will read it. Tone means how the writing sounds, such as friendly or formal. A source is where the facts come from. A limit tells the tool what it should avoid. You may also see people assign AI a role, such as writing assistant. That can help explain the kind of help wanted, but it does not make the tool a qualified reviewer. I add details when they matter to the result. I do not need a long description of an imaginary expert to write a simple reminder.

slides.title: A clearer request
slides.lead: The same job with the useful details included
items: Job + source + audience + format + limits
slides.quote: Write a friendly reminder for scholarship applicants. Use only this note: “Applications close October 1.” Write one sentence. Keep the date exactly as written. Do not add links or promises.
slides.notes: This request still does one small job. I have added who the message is for, the information it may use, and the form I want. Format means the shape of the answer. Here that shape is one sentence; later it will be a table. I have also named what must remain unchanged. I will compare this answer with the first one. The longer request is useful only if those added details improve what we need. A short request can work well. We should judge the answer by the task, rather than assume more words always produce a better result.

panels: Write a friendly reminder for scholarship applicants.
One sentence. No extra links or promises.
infographic.alt: Three large stations connected by arrows: a writing hand with a task note and audience silhouette; an open source notebook with a calendar; a short answer sheet beside a boundary marker. Show job and audience, original facts, answer format and limits.

slides.title: What a good answer looks like
slides.lead: Evaluation criteria are the checks we choose in advance.
items: Correct date: October 1
Requested format: one sentence
No added rules, links, or promises
slides.quote: Prepared example: “A friendly reminder: scholarship applications close October 1.”
slides.notes: Evaluation criteria is a formal phrase for the checks we use to judge an answer. In this example, we have only three: keep the date, use one sentence, and avoid adding information. The answer on this slide is a prepared teaching example, not a captured response from a live model. Your actual response may use different wording. That is fine if it passes the checks. I will ask a participant to inspect the date and someone else to look for an added promise. When we later use a scoring guide, we will make those checks just as visible.

panels: No extra rules, links, or promises.
infographic.alt: Three large checks side by side: a magnifying glass compares a calendar on two matching documents; a single short line of writing in an outlined one-sentence frame; a shield beside a document with extra lines visibly crossed out. Large clear checkmark with each. No text.

slides.title: Improving a request
slides.lead: A short practice cycle
table: Add the facts and limits that matter
Compare the answer with my checks
Fix a problem; keep the useful request
slides.notes: This practice cycle adapts the four-step prompt builder in my Creating with Generative AI materials, especially pages 24, 38, 39, and 42. First I choose a task. Then I write a request with the information needed for that task. I try it and compare the answer with the checks I chose. If something is wrong or unclear, I change the request and try again. Saving a useful request can save work next time, but I still need to check each new answer. I invite you to name one office task small enough to try this way. A reminder or a short checklist is a good starting point.

slides.title: Examples and follow-up requests
slides.lead: You can show the style you want and ask for a change.
items: An example shows the kind of answer I want.
A follow-up improves the answer I just received.
A sequence of small requests is often called prompt chaining.
slides.quote: Follow-up: “Make it warmer. Keep one sentence and keep October 1 unchanged.”
slides.notes: You can talk to the tool again after the first answer. This follow-up asks for a warmer tone while preserving the date and length. An example can also help: I might show one reminder in the style I like and ask for another with the supplied facts. You may hear zero-shot for no example, one-shot for one example, and few-shot for a few examples. Those names are optional vocabulary. The useful idea is showing what you mean. Prompt chaining means dividing work into connected requests. We can draft a reminder, check its facts, and then adjust its tone.

panels: An example makes the style you want clearer.
infographic.alt: An example sheet and small writing pen at left; two speech bubbles exchanging a short follow-up request in the middle; a revised document at right with a calendar symbol carried forward unchanged. A clear horizontal progression with an improvement loop from revised document toward the conversation. No text.

slides.title: AI can add a false detail
slides.lead: A confident answer still needs a fact check.
items: Original: “I ran 12 tutoring sessions.”
AI added: “Grades improved by 20%.”
The original does not support the added claim.
slides.notes: This picture shows a mistake we can check without special expertise. The original says the applicant ran twelve tutoring sessions. The AI draft adds an improvement in grades, but the original never says that. I would remove the extra claim and check the rest of the answer. People sometimes call an invented AI detail a hallucination. My earlier deck uses that term on page 59. The practical response is to compare it with the original information. Asking AI to say how confident it feels does not supply the missing evidence. Asking it to review its own answer can help find problems, but a person still needs to check the facts.
slides.alt: A person compares the original 12 sessions with an AI draft and crosses out an unsupported claim about grades.

panels: Remove the added claim. Check the other details.
infographic.alt: Left a source page and tutoring-book icon; middle an AI draft page with an extra bright coral line and a magnifying glass calling attention to it; right a person crosses out the extra coral line while keeping the original teal lines. Clear source-to-draft-to-correction arrows. No numerical chart or improvement illustration that suggests the false claim is true.

slides.title: Files in the practice packet
slides.lead: File endings tell us what kind of file we are opening.
table: A simple table, such as the application records
Plain text with simple headings; called Markdown
Plain text, such as a saved prompt
A document with a fixed page layout
slides.notes: The practice packet is a folder of small files you can open and inspect. CSV holds a simple table, with one row per record. Markdown, usually ending in dot md, is ordinary text with simple marks for headings or lists. TXT is plain text. A PDF preserves a document’s page layout. This builds on the file examples on pages 27 to 30 of my earlier deck. There is no single file type that guarantees AI will read everything correctly. If a file cannot be read, stop that part of the task and say what is missing. In our packet, the listed pretend PDFs are not included; the actual exercise uses the small text and CSV files.

slides.title: A person owns the decision
slides.lead: AI can prepare a checklist. Staff check it and decide.
items: Use the AI account and information your organization allows.
Names removed from a file do not remove every identifying detail.
Practice here uses made-up information.
slides.notes: Before I supply real applicant information, I need to know which account, tool, and task my organization allows. Removing names is not enough, because stories, schools, or other details may identify a person. I will use made-up information for every demonstration today. AI can help prepare a list of questions or point out a late date. A staff member checks the actual records and applies the organization’s rules. Staff also own final scores and award decisions. The picture shows the relationship I want: the computer supplies a checklist, and the person checks it before making a decision.
slides.alt: An AI checklist sits beside a staff member who checks it and records the decision.

panels: Use the account and information your organization allows.
Removing names may leave identifying details.
Staff check the records, scores, and final decisions.
infographic.alt: Left an organization-approved account shown as a work laptop with a permission key; middle a hand selects only a small needed part from a source file while other pages remain outside the upload area; right a staff member with a pen checks an AI checklist and records the decision. Clear process arrows. No promise of perfect security, no robot decision maker.

slides.title: Applicant codes in our examples
slides.lead: A17, A18, and A19 are made-up labels used instead of names.
items: The same code connects one applicant’s records.
A17-transcript.pdf means the transcript file for applicant A17.
A code alone does not make real information anonymous.
slides.notes: I want to explain these labels before we use the packet. A17 is a made-up applicant code, not a person you are expected to recognize. A18 and A19 represent two other made-up applicants. The same code appears across the files so we can connect each person’s records without using a name. For example, A17-transcript dot pdf means the transcript file associated with applicant A17. Using a code can reduce direct identification, but it does not remove every identifying detail in a real application. Our workshop files contain made-up information, so no actual applicant is involved.
slides.alt: One applicant has the code A17 on each of their matching documents.

panels: A17, A18, and A19 are made-up applicant labels.
A code alone does not make real data anonymous.
infographic.alt: Left one generic applicant silhouette on an application; center a large blank code tag replaces the name field; right matching blank code tags connect that applicant's record, transcript sheet, and reference sheet. One consistent tag shape links the same person, distinct from other applicants in the background. No text, no lock or anonymity promise.

slides.title: A manifest is a file list
slides.lead: A listed file name tells us what to look for.
items: manifest.csv lists pretend document names.
The pretend PDFs are not included.
A person must open an actual document to check its contents.
slides.notes: Manifest is another word that can sound more complicated than it is. Here it means a file list. Our manifest lists pretend filenames for each applicant. Seeing A17-transcript dot pdf on the list tells us that the name appears there. It does not tell us what grades are in that transcript or whether the transcript meets a requirement. In fact, those pretend PDFs are not included. We are practicing how to organize a list and identify questions for staff. I will stop any answer that claims to have read one of those unavailable documents.
slides.alt: A file list names A17-transcript.pdf beside a document that still needs to be opened.

panels: Our list names pretend PDF files.
Those pretend PDFs are not included.
Check the contents before relying on them.
infographic.alt: Left a catalog sheet lists generic file icons; middle a closed document folder with a large question mark; right a person opens and inspects the actual document with a magnifying glass. Show that a listing and the document contents are separate. No automatic checkmark on the closed folder.

slides.title: Words in a scoring guide
slides.lead: A rubric describes how to award points.
table: The part we are judging, such as community contribution
The description of what earns a particular score
The original words or facts supporting a score
A suggested score for a person to check
slides.notes: A rubric is a scoring guide. A criterion is one part of that guide, such as community contribution. An anchor describes the evidence needed for a particular score. Evidence is the original information supporting the judgment, and we need to know where to find it. A provisional score is a suggestion that a person must check; it is not a final decision. I will use these words on the practice page because they appear in the saved prompts. When we reach the scoring exercise, I will show the whole guide so nobody needs to guess what the scores mean.

slides.title: Our three ChatGPT demonstrations
slides.lead: One task at a time, with a person checking the answer
table: Every item on the original file list
Original words and the scoring rule
slides.notes: Now we can connect the introductory ideas with the office examples. The first task organizes filenames for each applicant. The second compares the listed items and dates with the made-up program rules. The third compares applicant statements with one part of a scoring guide. Each task has its own prompt and named input files. I will start a separate chat for each task so we can see what information it uses. The practice page has copyable prompts and prepared examples if a live run is unavailable. Those examples are teaching material, not proof of what a model will produce.

slides.title: Starting the practice in ChatGPT
slides.lead: A fresh chat is enough for these exercises.
items: Download and unzip the practice packet.
Start a new chat and supply only the files named for that task.
Paste the supplied instructions, then the task prompt.
Compare the answer with the original files.
slides.notes: I will download and unzip the practice packet first. For a basic run, I can open a fresh ChatGPT chat, paste the shared instructions, and add only the files named for that demonstration. Then I copy the task prompt and send it. If the account offers Projects, I can keep the same instructions and files together in a practice Project; I will explain that after the demonstrations. A Project is optional for getting started. The important part is making the named sources available and checking the answer against them. I will never upload real applicant information in this workshop.

panels: A Project is optional for getting started.
Add the instructions and only the named files.
Paste the prompt. Compare the answer with the files.
infographic.alt: Three stations: a person opens a blank chat on a laptop; a hand adds a small bundle of fictional source pages and a rules clipboard to the chat; the person compares the returned draft with the original pages using a magnifying glass. A clear left-to-right beginner setup. No account-specific buttons or UI labels.

slides.title: Demo 1: organizing application files
slides.lead: The job is to make the file list easier to inspect.
items: Files: manifest.csv and applications.csv
The practice page provides the full copyable prompt.
slides.quote: For each applicant code, list the file names, note any gaps in the list, and show where you found the information. Do not decide who qualifies.
link: Open and copy the full organization prompt
slides.notes: This slide gives the plain-language task. The practice page has the full prompt, including the fields and limits. I will attach manifest dot csv and applications dot csv, then copy that full prompt. We expect one row for each of the three applicant codes. We also expect every one of the twelve entries on the file list to remain accounted for. AI may point out a missing listing, but it cannot tell us that an unavailable document meets the rules. I will ask participants to count the applicant codes and check one row against the original list.

panels: Keep A17, A18, A19, and all 12 listed entries.
Staff verify the actual documents and any gaps.
infographic.alt: A loose pile of application documents at left is grouped into three distinct applicant folders in the middle; at right all three folders align beside a source-linked checklist and a person inspecting the list. Use three consistently colored folders but no names or numbers. Include a small question marker for a gap, not an eligibility ranking.

slides.title: Demo 1: checking the file list
slides.lead: Prepared teaching example; compare your actual answer with the files.
slides.notes: This table highlights what to check in the organization result. It is a shortened prepared example, not the complete inventory and not a captured AI response. The full prepared example on the practice page includes source locations. A17 has the required document types listed. A18 has no reference listed. A19 has no transcript listed and has an exception request, meaning a request for extra time or another allowed change. The complete inventory should still preserve the other listed files, including each application record. I will open the original list and verify those statements with the group.

slides.title: Demo 2: checking office records
slides.lead: AI can flag a missing item or late date for staff.
items: Files: program-rules.md, manifest.csv, applications.csv
Fictional deadline: October 1, 2026
slides.quote: Compare the listed items and application dates with the program rules. Show the rule and the original record for each concern. Staff decide what happens next.
link: Open and copy the full administrative prompt
slides.notes: For the second demonstration, I will add the program rules as well as the file list and application records. The made-up deadline is October 1, 2026. The rules require a statement, a transcript, and at least one reference. The task is to compare the records with those rules and flag questions. It is not to accept or reject applications. I will look for the exact rule and the row supporting each concern. If the tool cannot read a file, it needs to identify that problem rather than continue as if it had seen the contents.

panels: Flag a missing listing or a late recorded date.
A person decides exceptions and next steps.
infographic.alt: Left program rules on a clipboard with a calendar and required-document symbols; middle a person compares an application date and file list with the rules using a magnifying glass; right a missing page symbol and a clock beside a human staff review tray, not a rejection bin. Clear sequence from rules to comparison to staff follow-up.

slides.title: Demo 2: the late application
slides.lead: A19 is the applicant code for this made-up case.
items: A staff member applies the rules and records the reason.
table: Staff need to review the request
Staff need to check the actual records
slides.notes: I will focus on A19, our made-up applicant who submitted after the deadline and requested an exception. The recorded date is October 2. AI can report that the date is later than October 1 and that an exception request exists. It can also report that the file list has no transcript entry. A staff member must check the actual records and decide whether the rules allow extra time or another exception. I will watch for an answer that rejects A19 automatically. That would go beyond the task, even if the tool copied the date correctly.

slides.title: The community contribution scoring guide
slides.lead: Each anchor describes what earns that score.
table: Activity named, but applicant role unclear
Specific contribution and a supported result
slides.notes: Here is the complete made-up scoring guide for the third demonstration. Zero means the statement describes no relevant activity. One means an activity appears, but the applicant’s role is unclear. Two means the applicant describes a specific contribution. Three requires that contribution and a supported result. The guide judges contribution, so polished language alone does not earn extra points. I will read these descriptions aloud before asking for any score. We need the actual descriptions available to the model, and a human reviewer must check the suggested match against both the guide and the original statement.

slides.title: Demo 3: matching words to the guide
slides.lead: A suggested score needs a quote and a reason.
items: Files: statements.md and rubric.md
Source location = where to find the original words
slides.quote: Compare A17 and A18 with the community contribution guide. Quote the original words, suggest a score, and explain what information is missing. A person checks the score.
link: Open and copy the full scoring prompt
slides.notes: I will supply the statements and the complete rubric, then copy the full prompt from the practice page. We are comparing A17 and A18, which are our made-up applicant codes. I want the original quotation, its section, the suggested score, and an explanation using the guide. I also want to know what evidence is missing for the next score. The prompt calls the score provisional, which means a person must check it. We should not infer character or rank the applicants from these excerpts. I will verify each quoted word before discussing the suggested score.

panels: Quote the statement and show where to find it.
Suggest a score using the supplied descriptions.
Explain missing information. Staff own the score.
infographic.alt: Left a magnifying glass highlights a short line on an applicant statement; center a scoring-guide sheet has four simple unnumbered rows and a pointer matching one row; right a human reviewer with a pen checks the quote and guide beside a question marker for missing evidence. No medal, award ranking, personality inference, numerical chart, or automatic final score.

slides.title: The same work earns the same contribution score
slides.lead: Prepared teaching comparison
items: Both describe a specific contribution.
Neither excerpt supplies a supported result.
table: 12 tutoring days; got 2 volunteers to help
slides.notes: These statements use different wording for equivalent contribution evidence. Both describe twelve tutoring sessions or days and recruiting two volunteers. Under this guide, both support a suggested score of two. Neither excerpt supplies a supported result, so we do not have the evidence needed for three. The comparison is prepared teaching material, and these shortened phrases are summaries; the original wording is in statements dot md. I will compare the actual quotations there. If AI gives different scores, I will ask which fact in the contribution guide explains the difference. Writing polish alone cannot supply a greater contribution.

slides.title: A ChatGPT Project
slides.lead: A place to keep related chats, files, and instructions together
items: Optional next step: Scholarship Review Practice
slides.notes: A Project is a way to keep related work together. Instead of providing the same practice files and standing instructions in every new chat, I can put them in a practice Project when the account supports that feature. Each task can still have its own chat. The Project does not guarantee that the answer is correct, and it does not give us permission to upload applicant data. I will use the fictional packet and name the sources needed for each task. If Projects are unavailable, the fresh-chat method we already used remains a useful way to practice.

infographic.alt: Three stations connected by continuous teal lines inside one large open folder: overlapping empty speech bubbles for related chats; a bundle of source documents including a table page; a pinned instructions checklist. One enclosing folder keeps chats, files, and instructions together. No product logo, no automatic truth verification.

slides.title: Instructions for repeated work
slides.lead: Instructions are the rules I want AI to follow.
items: A prompt names today’s task.
Project instructions apply to work inside that Project.
slides.quote: Use only the supplied practice files. Show the original words and where to find them. Say when information is missing. Leave final decisions to staff.
link: Read or copy the complete practice instructions
slides.notes: Instructions are rules for how the work should happen. This short example explains the most important ideas in the complete practice instructions. A prompt tells the tool what I need on this occasion. Project instructions keep relevant rules with the ongoing practice work. Personal custom instructions can express preferences across chats, but private program details should stay with the appropriate task or Project. I will inspect every answer even when instructions are saved. If a source document contains a request to ignore our rules, that is part of the source text to examine, not permission to change the review process.

panels: Quote the original and say where to find it.
Saved instructions still need human checks.
infographic.alt: Three clear stations: a small stack of supplied source files within a marked boundary; a magnifying glass connects an answer's quote to the original document; a human staff member holds the final-decision pen while an AI checklist sits nearby. A connected ribbon suggests the same standing rules persist across tasks. No text.

slides.title: A skill is a reusable recipe
slides.lead: It saves the steps for a task I expect to repeat.
table: An applicant excerpt and the scoring guide
Try examples where I know the answer
slides.notes: I think of a skill as a reusable recipe. This builds on the reusable-instruction steps on pages 61, 62, and 70 of my earlier deck. It describes what information is needed, how to carry out the task, and how to check the result. Our evidence-review skill asks for a statement and a scoring guide, then returns quotations, a suggested match, and missing information for a person to check. We can try the written procedure manually in a chat. Tools differ in how they install and run skills, so I do not assume one installation method works everywhere. Before relying on it, I will try known examples, missing information, and a misleading instruction inside a source.

slides.title: Fair rules for applicant use of AI
slides.lead: Applicants need clear expectations before they apply.
items: State what help is allowed and what must be disclosed.
A tool’s “AI-written” flag can be wrong.
Staff check concerns and give applicants a fair chance to explain.
slides.notes: Our review process also needs clear expectations for applicants. We should publish what kinds of help are allowed and how applicants should disclose that help. If a detection tool flags an essay, the flag does not prove who wrote it or that a rule was broken. An unflagged essay is not proof either. Staff should examine the concern under the published policy, give the applicant a fair chance to explain, and record the decision. The practice page includes sample language for local discussion. Each organization still needs to decide its own rules and how someone can request another review.

panels: Say what help is allowed and what to disclose.
Staff follow the rules and let the applicant explain.
infographic.alt: Left published applicant rules on a document handed to a person before they start writing; middle a detector-like magnifying glass with a question mark beside an essay, clearly uncertain rather than a guilty stamp; right two people have a respectful clarification conversation beside a human review record. No automatic rejection, cheating symbol, or accusation.

slides.title: My next small practice task
slides.lead: One request I can check myself
items: Choose one made-up note or practice file.
Write the result I want and what must stay accurate.
Check the answer against the original.
Keep the request and note what I had to fix.
slides.notes: I invite you to choose one small task to try after the session. You can use the reminder example, the file-list demonstration, or one statement and the scoring guide. Write down the result you want and what you will check before you send the request. After the answer appears, compare it with the original. Keep a note of anything you changed, including a false detail, a missing item, or an unclear instruction. Then try again with that improvement. You can revisit the self-check and choose one next step. There is no need to master every feature before practicing one useful task.

panels: Use a made-up note or one practice file.
Keep the useful request and note what you fixed.
infographic.alt: Left a person chooses one small fictional note and writes a brief request; middle they compare an AI draft with the source using a magnifying glass; right they save the useful request and a small correction note in a folder. Clear circular arrow suggests trying again after checking. No trophy, expertise badge, or guarantee of correctness.

slides.title: Practice and reference materials
slides.lead: The participant page brings the materials together.
items: Presentation PDF and a plain-language word guide
Copyable ChatGPT prompts and made-up practice files
Awareness self-check and further examples
slides.notes: The participant page contains the presentation PDF, a word guide, the three demonstrations, and the fictional practice packet. Each demonstration names the files it needs, supplies a copyable prompt, and includes a prepared example for comparison. The awareness self-check gives a small next step if you want more practice. The QR code leads to the broader NSPA resource post, and the direct practice link opens this collection. You can also explore The Prompt Library and The Skills Library when you want more examples. I encourage you to begin with one task whose answer you can check, then build from what you learn.
